entities.name: Abercius of Hieropolis
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Abercius of Hieropolis (c. 130–200 CE) was a Christian bishop of Hieropolis in Phrygia (modern Turkey) who lived during the reign of Marcus Aurelius and is venerated as a saint in both the Catholic and Orthodox traditions. He is primarily known through the remarkable Abercius Inscription — a funerary epitaph he reportedly composed for himself that is considered one of the oldest and most important documents of early Christian history.

The Abercius Inscription, discovered in 1882 and now in the Vatican Museums, describes a journey Abercius made to Rome and Syria, using symbolic language to describe encountering Christian communities, receiving Eucharist ('fish from a spring, large and pure, caught by a holy virgin'), and meeting Christians everywhere from Rome to the Syrian plain. The inscription's coded language — necessary under Roman persecution — provides extraordinary evidence for the geographical spread of Christian communities and Eucharistic practice in the second century.

Scholars have debated the inscription's interpretation since its discovery, but the scholarly consensus regards it as a genuine second-century Christian document of exceptional historical importance. Abercius is also associated with a later legendary life that credits him with miraculous healings and the expulsion of demons. His feast day is celebrated on 22 October in both the Roman and Byzantine traditions.
